title: La Traviata
facts: Today’s matinee is the Met’s 1,042nd Traviata. New York first heard it in 1856, at the Academy of Music.
Host Renée Fleming sang Violetta at the Met in 2003, and again on the Met’s tour to Japan in 2006.
The prelude opens on very soft, very high strings, the frail heroine. Then the love theme, on lower strings.
Director Michael Mayer won a Tony for Spring Awakening. His Traviata opened at the Met in December 2018.
Curtain up, and lively dance tunes take over. Waltz rhythms run through all of Act I: Paris, in three-quarter time.
La traviata is the only one of Verdi’s many operas set entirely indoors.
The Brindisi: a drinking song in B-flat major, in a lilting 3/8, marked Allegretto.
That offstage band? Verdi sketched its waltzes like a piano score and left the scoring to the bandmaster.
Stephen Costello, our Alfredo, made his Met debut on the 2007–08 opening night, as Arturo in Lucia.
^Act\ I:\ È\ strano!—Ah,\ fors'è\ lui\ che\ l'anima$
Nadine Sierra at the Met: Ilia in Idomeneo (2017), then Susanna in Figaro the next season. Now, Violetta.
“Sempre libera” is all feverish ornamentation. Savor it: Violetta never needs coloratura again after Act I.
Verdi wanted a modern-dress setting. La Fenice insisted on the past: “c. 1700”.
Dumas fils turned his 1848 novel into the 1852 play La Dame aux camélias. Verdi’s opera followed in 1853.
The great Germont–Violetta duet begins: many sections, the music turning with every shift in the drama.
^Act\ II:\ Un\ dì,\ quando\ le\ veneri$
Luca Salsi, our Germont, once sang twice at the Met in a day: Ernani on 30 minutes’ notice, then Lucia.
At the Venice premiere, Act II is where the audience turned. Verdi next day: “La traviata last night a failure.”
Verdi to his friend Emanuele Muzio, the day after the premiere (6 March 1853)
Violetta’s music has traveled: hectic coloratura in Act I, drama in Act II, and now a spiritual quality.
Revised, it triumphed in Venice in 1854. Librettist Piave: “Then it was a fiasco; now it has created a furore.”
Francesco Maria Piave, on the revival at Venice’s Teatro San Benedetto, 6 May 1854
^Act\ III:\ Teneste\ la\ promessa\ \.\.\.\ Addio\ del\ passato$
Nadine Sierra received the 2018 Beverly Sills Artist Award, in a ceremony held right here at the Met.
A whale of a credit: in 2010 Stephen Costello created Greenhorn (Ishmael) in Jake Heggie’s Moby-Dick.
